architectural_implications.after: Each tool call is adjudicated against mission context, budget, and policy at execution time, with short-lived, use-limited credentials.
architectural_implications.before: OAuth consent screen grants a broad scope set at login; the token is then a bearer capability for the whole session.
architectural_implications.consequence: The tool-execution layer becomes a policy enforcement point and must carry mission/intent context; token issuance becomes a function of intent rather than of app identity.
architectural_implications.observation: Authorization moves from session-establishment to per-invocation enforcement.

architectural_implications.after: A supervisory/worker split plus a deterministic policy layer outside the LLM decides what the hands may do.
architectural_implications.before: The agent process holds credentials and is trusted to use them appropriately, with guardrails expressed as prompts.
architectural_implications.consequence: Guardrails become testable software artifacts with deterministic behavior rather than prompt heuristics, and the reasoning model can be swapped or compromised without changing the security posture.
architectural_implications.observation: The model is removed from the trusted computing base for permissions.

architectural_implications.after: Tools are designed so the smallest authorizable unit maps to a meaningful human intent.
architectural_implications.before: Tools are designed for model convenience and capability breadth (get_database, generic fetch).
architectural_implications.consequence: Tool schemas must be co-designed with policy; broad tools either cannot be safely exposed or must be wrapped in finer-grained sub-operations.
architectural_implications.observation: Tool/API interface granularity becomes a security-sensitive design surface.

architectural_implications.after: Agents present verifiable delegation credentials enabling per-agent trust, rate limits, and accountability.
architectural_implications.before: Platforms authenticate browsers and users; anything else is indistinguishable from a bot and handled by IP/UA blocking.
architectural_implications.consequence: Platforms need selective admission for agents, and agent runtimes need to expose identity that downstream services can verify — a standards gap, not a product feature.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent identity becomes a first-class federation problem for web platforms.

article_ideas.angle: Argue from the determinism mismatch rather than from scope coarseness, and show that 'just add more scopes' is a category error by predicting the exact failure mode of each static design.
article_ideas.audience: Platform engineers and identity/security architects building agent products on top of existing OAuth infrastructure
article_ideas.based_on: Agentic workflows are non-deterministic; you cannot know agent requirements ahead of time.
article_ideas.thesis: The failure of OAuth for agents is structural, not a scoping-tuning problem: OAuth enumerates resource needs at design time, while an agent's requirement set is discovered at runtime by the model. Every static-permission agent platform therefore faces a forced choice between over-granting and breaking, and no amount of narrower scopes escapes it.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Is Not an App: The Determinism Mismatch That Breaks OAuth

article_ideas.angle: Make it an engineering-consequence argument: the get_page vs get_database split is a security boundary, and every 'convenient' generic tool is an unauthorized capability bundle.
article_ideas.audience: MCP server authors and API designers exposing tools to agents
article_ideas.based_on: Notion MCP server tool calls like get_page vs get_database.
article_ideas.thesis: Policy expressiveness is bounded by interface design. Because coarse MCP tools bundle semantically distinct capabilities like reading one page and enumerating a database, humans cannot author meaningful policy at the tool level, and no runtime engine fixes that. Tool surfaces must be co-designed with authorization semantics, meaning broad tools either cannot be safely exposed or must be wrapped into finer sub-operations.
article_ideas.title: The Smallest Authorizable Unit: Your Tool Schema Is Your Security Policy

article_ideas.angle: Reframe blocking as a symptom of a missing standard, and show that the cost of the missing credential is paid by the human delegator, which is the wrong incentive for the ecosystem.
article_ideas.audience: Consumer-platform trust & safety teams, agent-runtime builders, and identity-standards people
article_ideas.based_on: An Instinct agent made 200 API calls an hour trying to book a restaurant on Resy and got the user banned.
article_ideas.thesis: When platforms cannot distinguish a legitimate delegated agent from a scraper, they can only respond with blunt denial, and the penalty lands on the principal rather than the agent. The Resy account ban and IP-sharing blocks are not abuse-prevention successes but evidence of an accountability inversion caused by the absence of a verifiable delegation credential.
article_ideas.title: The Ban Is the Bug: How Missing Agent Identity Inverts Liability

article_ideas.angle: Apply the classic reference-monitor requirement to agent stacks and treat prompt-based guardrails as an anti-pattern with a specific failure mode: self-persuasion.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework authors and security engineers reviewing agent architectures
article_ideas.based_on: Separating the worker agent from a supervisory agent provides necessary checks and balances.
article_ideas.thesis: A supervisory agent is still an LLM, so oversight built only from supervisors inherits the non-determinism it is meant to constrain. The enforceable boundary must be a deterministic decision point outside the model's influence; otherwise a compromised or hallucinating model can reason its way around its own guardrails, and the guardrail is not a testable software artifact.
article_ideas.title: Guardrails Must Not Be Generatable: Why the Policy Layer Has to Sit Outside the Model

connections.relationship: The agentic restatement of classic mandatory-access-control enforcement: decide at the point of action, from a trusted, non-bypassable component.
Intent is what a delegation credential must encode so downstream services can verify purpose, not just identity.
Same mechanism moved inside the agent runtime: an enforced resource ceiling that converts runaway behavior into a bounded stop.
Both stem from the absence of verifiable delegation, which is why platforms answer with blanket blocking.

evidence_quotes.text: Runtime auth authorizes an agent per tool call rather than granting broad static access.
Intent-Based Authorization Framework

core_insights.generalization: For any non-deterministic executor (agents, generated SQL, generated shell), put the authorization boundary at the individual action, not at session bootstrap.
core_insights.insight: Authorization should move from static, pre-granted scopes to a runtime decision made per tool call, evaluated against the agent's stated mission plus live constraints. The grant is not 'this app may read your data' but 'this specific call, under this intent, within these limits, is allowed now.'
core_insights.why_it_matters: Static scopes are issued before the agent's behavior is known, so any autonomy granted is strictly wider than any single legitimate action. Moving the enforcement point to the tool-call boundary narrows the blast radius of a misbehaving agent without removing its usefulness.

evidence_quotes.text: OAuth was designed for browser-based redirects and static website-to-website communication.
Agentic workflows are non-deterministic; you cannot know agent requirements ahead of time.
Traditional IAM is built for deterministic human workflows, whereas agents operate dynamically and non-deterministically.

core_insights.generalization: Whenever the consumer of a permission system is itself a planner, permission design must shift from enumeration to runtime adjudication.
core_insights.insight: The root cause is a mismatch of determinism: OAuth/IAM was designed for software whose resource needs are enumerable at design time, while agentic workflows cannot enumerate their requirements in advance. This makes the gap structural, not a scoping-tuning problem.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Explains why 'just add more scopes' or 'just make narrower scopes' fails — the requirement set is discovered at runtime by the model, so no static scope set is correct. It predicts that any static-permission agent platform will either over-grant or break.

evidence_quotes.text: Coarse-grained MCP tools and APIs make human policy-writing difficult.
Notion MCP server tool calls like get_page vs get_database.

core_insights.generalization: API/tool surface design is a security design decision; the granularity of your tool schema determines the granularity of your enforceable policy.
core_insights.insight: Tool granularity, not just token granularity, is a policy-authoring bottleneck: coarse MCP tools bundle semantically different capabilities (reading one page vs. enumerating an entire database), so a human cannot express a meaningful policy at the tool level.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Even a perfect runtime policy engine is useless if the smallest authorizable unit is a tool that conflates read-one with read-all. Policy expressiveness is bounded by interface design, so agent-facing tools must be designed with authorization semantics in mind.

evidence_quotes.text: Decoupling the LLM reasoning layer ('brains') from execution tools ('hands') creates safety boundaries.
Separating the worker agent from a supervisory agent provides necessary checks and balances.
Deterministic policy layers outside the LLM govern agent permissions.

core_insights.generalization: Apply the classic reference-monitor pattern to agents: the policy decision point must be deterministic and outside the model's influence, or the model can reason its way around its own guardrails.
core_insights.insight: Split the agent into an unprivileged reasoning component ('brains') and a privileged execution component ('hands'), with a supervisory agent and a deterministic, non-LLM policy layer adjudicating between them.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It prevents a compromised or hallucinating model from directly holding credentials or execution capability, and it makes policy enforcement auditable because the decision path is not itself generative.

evidence_quotes.text: Tokens with time limits and resource budgets expiring after use.
Budgets and time limitations control resource consumption and prevent infinite loops.

core_insights.generalization: Any autonomous loop should consume a finite, meterable allowance (time, calls, money) that the runtime enforces, as a control that does not depend on model self-restraint.
core_insights.insight: Credentials should be budgeted, not just scoped: tokens carry time limits and resource budgets and expire after use, turning runaway loops into a bounded, self-terminating failure.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Gives a hard, verifiable ceiling on cost and downstream load independent of model judgment — the failure mode becomes 'agent stops' rather than 'agent exhausts the account or gets the user banned.'

evidence_quotes.text: Unauthenticated clients (like web scraping bots or automated scripts) face similar identity problems.
An Instinct agent made 200 API calls an hour trying to book a restaurant on Resy and got the user banned.
Vercel being blocked in Spain due to IP sharing and lack of agent identity.

core_insights.generalization: Delegated autonomy requires a verifiable delegation credential; without it, downstream systems can only respond with coarse denial, and reputational/financial cost flows to the delegator.
core_insights.insight: Agent identity is the same problem as the unauthenticated-client / bot problem: because the web has no way to distinguish a legitimate agent acting for a principal from a scraper, both get treated identically — blocked or banned — and the penalty lands on the principal, not the agent.
core_insights.why_it_matters: The Resy case shows the accountability inversion: the agent's misbehavior (200 calls/hour) is absorbed by the human account. Without a distinguishable agent identity, platforms cannot rate-limit or trust selectively, so they default to blunt blocking that punishes legitimate delegation.

deep_dives.research_question: Where is the budget/expiry boundary at which runaway loops are reliably capped but legitimately long or retrying tasks still complete, and what does the agent do at the boundary — stop cleanly, or leave partial side effects?
deep_dives.topic: Budgeted credentials as a hard failure ceiling versus legitimate task completion
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Budgets and time limitations control resource consumption and prevent infinite loops.
deep_dives.why: Budgets convert an unbounded, model-judgment-dependent failure into a bounded, runtime-enforced stop, which is the only control that does not rely on model self-restraint. But a hard ceiling that aborts mid-transaction trades one incident class (exhaustion, bans) for another (partial writes, inconsistent state), and nobody has characterized that frontier.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Granularity at the transaction layer is required to audit and know what happened.
deep_dives.why: Attribution is claimed to follow from intent framing, but attribution that cannot be replayed is a legal posture without an engineering substrate. The audit triple is the concrete artifact that makes liability claims testable rather than rhetorical.

Run a red-team suite of agents instructed to exceed their mission, escalate scope, and socially engineer the supervisor.

project_ideas.name: Budget Frontier Sweep

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Allie Howe, Ian Livingstone, Michael Davis, Dick Hardt
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Intent-Based Auth and Runtime Authorization for AI Agents
  • Purpose: To explore the future of agent authentication, why traditional OIDC and OAuth fall short for AI agents, and how intent-based runtime auth can solve security, context, and liability challenges. A panel discussion at AI Engineer New York featuring leaders from Keycard, JPMorgan Chase, and AAuth discussing the limitations of traditional OAuth for AI agents, the necessity of intent-based authorization, runtime scoping, and managing security, liabilities, and human-in-the-loop workflows as agents gain autonomy in enterprise and consumer environments.

Topic Map

Introduction to Intent-Based Auth

  • Explanation: Panel introduction defining intent-based auth and why runtime authorization is becoming necessary as agents gain autonomy.
  • Key claims:
    • Companies want to give agents increased autonomy, requiring runtime authorization.
    • Runtime auth authorizes an agent per tool call rather than granting broad static access.
    • Coarse-grained MCP tools and APIs make human policy-writing difficult.
  • Examples:
    • Notion MCP server tool calls like get_page vs get_database.
  • Terminology:
    • Runtime Auth
    • Intent-Based Authorization
    • MCP
    • Agent Autonomy
  • Why it matters: Broad standing access leads to agent misuse and security failures.

Why OAuth and Traditional Auth Fall Short

  • Explanation: Analysis of why OAuth2, designed for web-to-web redirects and static scopes, is ill-equipped for non-deterministic AI agent behaviors.
  • Key claims:
    • OAuth was designed for browser-based redirects and static website-to-website communication.
    • Agentic workflows are non-deterministic; you cannot know agent requirements ahead of time.
    • OAuth scopes are too coarse-grained for agent operations.
  • Examples:
    • Salesforce API scopes on OAuth.
  • Terminology:
    • OAuth2
    • Scopes
    • Deterministic Software
    • Single Scope
  • Why it matters: Treating agents like traditional web applications creates severe security gaps.

The Mission and Context Problem

  • Explanation: Discussion on how missions and intent capture the broader picture around agent decisions.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents act on behalf of a person or organization (the 'person').
    • A mission defines what the agent is supposed to accomplish big-picture.
    • Granularity at the transaction layer is required to audit and know what happened.
  • Examples:
    • Making a payment transaction versus a broad scope.
  • Terminology:
    • Mission
    • Granularity
    • Transaction Layer
    • Agent Identity
  • Why it matters: Context and intent prevent agents from executing harmful or unintended actions.

Policy, Budgets, and Separation of Concerns

  • Explanation: How budgets and policy enforcement can restrict agent actions and prevent runaway loops.
  • Key claims:
    • Separating the worker agent from a supervisory agent provides necessary checks and balances.
    • Budgets and time limitations control resource consumption and prevent infinite loops.
    • Deterministic policy layers outside the LLM govern agent permissions.
  • Examples:
    • Tokens with time limits and resource budgets expiring after use.
  • Terminology:
    • Supervisory Agent
    • Separation of Concerns
    • Policy Enforcement
    • Budgets
    • Deterministic Policy
  • Why it matters: Without budgets and separation of concerns, agents can drain resources or cause catastrophic failures.

Agent Identity and Web Compatibility

  • Explanation: Addressing how the web wasn't built for agents and how agent identity mirrors unauthenticated client problems.
  • Key claims:
    • The web was built for humans using browsers, not autonomous agents.
    • Unauthenticated clients (like web scraping bots or automated scripts) face similar identity problems.
    • Federated protocols like OIDC and TLS enabled the web economy, but agent federation requires new standards.
  • Examples:
    • Vercel being blocked in Spain due to IP sharing and lack of agent identity.
  • Terminology:
    • Unauthenticated Client
    • Federation
    • OIDC
    • TLS
    • Guest Checkout
  • Why it matters: Web platforms need ways to distinguish and trust legitimate AI agents without blocking them entirely.

The Resy Incident and Practical Application

  • Explanation: Examining real-world incidents where agents went rogue and abused APIs.
  • Key claims:
    • An Instinct agent made 200 API calls an hour trying to book a restaurant on Resy and got the user banned.
    • Intent-based auth helps prevent agents from abusing downstream resources.
    • Cybersecurity has much to learn from robotics regarding situational awareness.
  • Examples:
    • Instinct agent getting a user's Resy account banned.
  • Terminology:
    • Instinct Agent
    • Resy
    • API Calls
    • Forensics
  • Why it matters: Unchecked agents can trigger real-world financial or reputational damage.

Key Points

Traditional Auth is Static, Agents are Dynamic

  • Explanation: Traditional IAM is built for deterministic human workflows, whereas agents operate dynamically and non-deterministically.
  • Evidence: OAuth scopes mapped to static enterprise applications.
  • Practical implication: Enterprises must transition to runtime authorization.

Separation of Brain and Hands

  • Explanation: Decoupling the LLM reasoning layer ('brains') from execution tools ('hands') creates safety boundaries.
  • Evidence: Supervisory agents evaluating worker agent actions against policy.
  • Practical implication: Prevents agents from executing unauthorized actions directly.

Psychological Ownership and Liability

  • Explanation: Intent creates psychological ownership and links human accountability to agent outcomes.
  • Evidence: Historical liability frameworks (e.g., IBM manuals) applied to AI employment.
  • Practical implication: The employer or user deploying the agent remains legally and ethically liable.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Intent-Based Authorization Framework

  • How it works: Authorizes agents dynamically per tool call based on overarching mission context and runtime constraints rather than static broad permissions.
  • Components:
    • Mission Identifier
    • Runtime Policy Evaluator
    • Supervisory Agent
    • Budget and Time Limits
  • When to use: Deploying enterprise AI agents with access to internal databases, financial tools, or external APIs.

Examples & Case Studies

An Instinct agent made 200 API calls in an hour trying to book a Resy reservation.

  • Illustrates: Unconstrained agent behavior exhausting downstream resources and getting a user banned.
  • Lesson: Agents require strict budgets, rate-limiting, and intent verification.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Audit existing OAuth scopes given to AI agents.
    • Implement runtime authorization checks for tool calls.
  • Strategic:
    • Adopt a 'brain and hands' separation architecture for agents.
    • Build federated agent identity standards across the industry.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we handle toxic combinations of agent capabilities?
    • Who is liable when an autonomous agent executes a damaging transaction?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • An Instinct agent made 200 API calls in an hour on Resy and got a user banned. (Anecdotal event)
  • Vercel was blocked in Spain due to IP sharing and scraping prevention measures. (Industry case study)

Notable Quotes

"Runtime auth is the practice of authorizing an agent per tool call, rather than having the agent hold broad standing access that it will eventually misuse." (at 0:58) "The web was not made for agents." (at 29:59)

Compressed Summary

  • OAuth and OIDC are too coarse-grained for non-deterministic AI agents.
  • Runtime authorization evaluates intent and context per tool call.
  • Separating the 'brain' (LLM) from the 'hands' (tools) via supervisory agents ensures safety.
  • Budgets and time limits prevent runaway agent loops and resource exhaustion.
  • Keywords: authentication, authorization, agents, oauth, security
  • Core insight: AI agents require intent-based runtime authorization and separation of concerns to safely operate without causing unintended damage or security breaches.

  - Coarse-grained MCP tools and APIs make human policy-writing difficult.
- **Examples**:
  - Notion MCP server tool calls like get_page vs get_database.
- **Terminology**:
  - Runtime Auth
  - Intent-Based Authorization
  - MCP
  - Agent Autonomy
- **Why it matters**: Broad standing access leads to agent misuse and security failures.
### Why OAuth and Traditional Auth Fall Short
- **Explanation**: Analysis of why OAuth2, designed for web-to-web redirects and static scopes, is ill-equipped for non-deterministic AI agent behaviors.
- **Key claims**:
  - OAuth was designed for browser-based redirects and static website-to-website communication.
  - Agentic workflows are non-deterministic; you cannot know agent requirements ahead of time.
  - OAuth scopes are too coarse-grained for agent operations.
- **Examples**:
  - Salesforce API scopes on OAuth.
- **Terminology**:
  - OAuth2
  - Scopes
  - Deterministic Software
  - Single Scope
- **Why it matters**: Treating agents like traditional web applications creates severe security gaps.
### The Mission and Context Problem
- **Explanation**: Discussion on how missions and intent capture the broader picture around agent decisions.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents act on behalf of a person or organization (the 'person').
  - A mission defines what the agent is supposed to accomplish big-picture.
  - Granularity at the transaction layer is required to audit and know what happened.
- **Examples**:
  - Making a payment transaction versus a broad scope.
- **Terminology**:
  - Mission
  - Granularity
  - Transaction Layer
  - Agent Identity
- **Why it matters**: Context and intent prevent agents from executing harmful or unintended actions.
### Policy, Budgets, and Separation of Concerns
- **Explanation**: How budgets and policy enforcement can restrict agent actions and prevent runaway loops.
- **Key claims**:
  - Separating the worker agent from a supervisory agent provides necessary checks and balances.
  - Budgets and time limitations control resource consumption and prevent infinite loops.
  - Deterministic policy layers outside the LLM govern agent permissions.
- **Examples**:
  - Tokens with time limits and resource budgets expiring after use.
- **Terminology**:
  - Supervisory Agent
  - Separation of Concerns
  - Policy Enforcement
  - Budgets
  - Deterministic Policy
- **Why it matters**: Without budgets and separation of concerns, agents can drain resources or cause catastrophic failures.
### Agent Identity and Web Compatibility
- **Explanation**: Addressing how the web wasn't built for agents and how agent identity mirrors unauthenticated client problems.
- **Key claims**:
  - The web was built for humans using browsers, not autonomous agents.
  - Unauthenticated clients (like web scraping bots or automated scripts) face similar identity problems.
  - Federated protocols like OIDC and TLS enabled the web economy, but agent federation requires new standards.
- **Examples**:
  - Vercel being blocked in Spain due to IP sharing and lack of agent identity.
- **Terminology**:
  - Unauthenticated Client
  - Federation
  - OIDC
  - TLS
  - Guest Checkout
- **Why it matters**: Web platforms need ways to distinguish and trust legitimate AI agents without blocking them entirely.
### The Resy Incident and Practical Application
- **Explanation**: Examining real-world incidents where agents went rogue and abused APIs.
- **Key claims**:
  - An Instinct agent made 200 API calls an hour trying to book a restaurant on Resy and got the user banned.
  - Intent-based auth helps prevent agents from abusing downstream resources.
  - Cybersecurity has much to learn from robotics regarding situational awareness.
- **Examples**:
  - Instinct agent getting a user's Resy account banned.
- **Terminology**:
  - Instinct Agent
  - Resy
  - API Calls
  - Forensics
- **Why it matters**: Unchecked agents can trigger real-world financial or reputational damage.
## Key Points
### Traditional Auth is Static, Agents are Dynamic
- **Explanation**: Traditional IAM is built for deterministic human workflows, whereas agents operate dynamically and non-deterministically.
- **Evidence**: OAuth scopes mapped to static enterprise applications.
- **Practical implication**: Enterprises must transition to runtime authorization.
### Separation of Brain and Hands
- **Explanation**: Decoupling the LLM reasoning layer ('brains') from execution tools ('hands') creates safety boundaries.
- **Evidence**: Supervisory agents evaluating worker agent actions against policy.
- **Practical implication**: Prevents agents from executing unauthorized actions directly.
### Psychological Ownership and Liability
- **Explanation**: Intent creates psychological ownership and links human accountability to agent outcomes.
- **Evidence**: Historical liability frameworks (e.g., IBM manuals) applied to AI employment.
- **Practical implication**: The employer or user deploying the agent remains legally and ethically liable.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Intent-Based Authorization Framework
- **How it works**: Authorizes agents dynamically per tool call based on overarching mission context and runtime constraints rather than static broad permissions.
- **Components**:
  - Mission Identifier
  - Runtime Policy Evaluator
  - Supervisory Agent
  - Budget and Time Limits
- **When to use**: Deploying enterprise AI agents with access to internal databases, financial tools, or external APIs.
## Examples & Case Studies
### An Instinct agent made 200 API calls in an hour trying to book a Resy reservation.
- **Illustrates**: Unconstrained agent behavior exhausting downstream resources and getting a user banned.
- **Lesson**: Agents require strict budgets, rate-limiting, and intent verification.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Audit existing OAuth scopes given to AI agents.
  - Implement runtime authorization checks for tool calls.
- **Strategic**:
  - Adopt a 'brain and hands' separation architecture for agents.
  - Build federated agent identity standards across the industry.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we handle toxic combinations of agent capabilities?
  - Who is liable when an autonomous agent executes a damaging transaction?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- An Instinct agent made 200 API calls in an hour on Resy and got a user banned. (Anecdotal event)
- Vercel was blocked in Spain due to IP sharing and scraping prevention measures. (Industry case study)
## Notable Quotes
> "Runtime auth is the practice of authorizing an agent per tool call, rather than having the agent hold broad standing access that it will eventually misuse." (at 0:58)
> "The web was not made for agents." (at 29:59)
## Compressed Summary
- OAuth and OIDC are too coarse-grained for non-deterministic AI agents.
- Runtime authorization evaluates intent and context per tool call.
- Separating the 'brain' (LLM) from the 'hands' (tools) via supervisory agents ensures safety.
- Budgets and time limits prevent runaway agent loops and resource exhaustion.
- **Keywords**: authentication, authorization, agents, oauth, security
- **Core insight**: AI agents require intent-based runtime authorization and separation of concerns to safely operate without causing unintended damage or security breaches.
